This section shows how to do [Exercise 1](../exercise1.qmd) using `git` via the command-line interface (CLI). See the linked exercise for the narrative.

### Part 1: Initializing and adding files

1. Go to your home directory by typing:

   ```bash
   cd
   ```

1. Create a directory called `test-git-repo` and `cd` into it:

   ```bash
   mkdir test-git-repo
   cd test-git-repo
   ```

1. Initialise a Git repository in this folder:

   ```bash
   git init
   ```

1. `test-git-repo` is now tracked by `git`. See its status with:

   ```bash
   git status
   ```

   You should get:

   ```bash
   On branch main

   No commits yet

   nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
   ```

1. Create a file called `story.txt` and add the following to it:

   ```bash
   Once upon a time, in a land far,
   far away...
   ```

   After saving the file, type `ls` to verify it's there. Now run:

   ```bash
   git status
   ```

   again. You should have:

   ```bash
   On branch main

   No commits yet

   Untracked files:
     (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
       story.txt

   nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
   ```

1. Run the following to tell Git to start tracking `story.txt`:

   ```bash
   git add story.txt
   ```

   Now type `git status`. You'll see:

   ```bash
   On branch main

   No commits yet

   Changes to be committed:
     (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
       new file:   story.txt
   ```

   `story.txt` not *committed* yet, it is *staged* for the next commit.

1. Commit the change by running:

   ```bash
   git commit -m "add story idea"
   ```

   `git status` should now give `nothing to commit, working tree clean`. 
   
   Congratulations, you've made your first commit! To verify, run:

   ```bash
   git log
   ```

   to see the history of your commits. Since this is your first commit, there will only be one entry.

### Part 2: Making changes to files

1. In `story.txt`, change the line `Once upon a time, in a land far,` to `A long time ago in a galaxy far,`. `git status` should now give:

   ```bash
   On branch main
   Changes not staged for commit:
     (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
     (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
       modified:   story.txt

   no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
   ```

   Our changes to `story.txt` have not been committed yet. `git diff` shows what changed since the last commit:

   ```bash
   git diff
   ```

1. Stage the changes using `git add`:

   ```bash
   git add story.txt
   ```

   (Use `git add -u` to stage changes to all tracked files that have changed.) 
   
   Commit the change without the `-m`:

   ```bash
   git commit
   ```

   This causes a text editor to open, and this is where you can add a commit message. This is useful if you want to write a multiline message. Type "change opening". Saving and exiting the file completes the commit and returns to the command line. To verify that the commit worked, run:

   ```bash
   git log
   ```

   You'll now see 2 commits in your history.

### Part 3: Branches

1. Run `git branch`. You should get back:

   ```bash
   * main
   ```

   because we currently have only one branch, called `main`. The `*` next to `main` means that you are currently on the main branch. Create a new branch to work on the titles:

   ```bash
   git checkout -b title-dev
   ```

   `git checkout` allows us to navigate to a new branch. Adding `-b` means that this command must create the branch before navigating to it.

   You'll get `Switched to a new branch 'title-dev'`. To verify, run `git branch` again. Now you should see:

   ```bash
     main
   * title-dev
   ```

1. Create `title.txt` and add:

   ```bash
   STAR FIGHT!
   ```

1. `git status` shows that `title.txt` is untracked. Add it to be tracked and commit:

   ```bash
   git add title.txt
   git commit -m "add title idea"
   ```

   Now type `git log`; you'll see you have 3 commits in your history.

1. Go back to the `main` branch with:

   ```bash
   git checkout main
   ```

   `git branch` shows:

   ```bash
   * main
     title-dev
   ```

   Running `ls` shows that `title.txt` is gone, and indeed `git log` only shows the first two commits. The commit we just created only lives on `title-dev`.

   ::: {.callout-tip title="Graph view in the terminal" collapse="true"}
   You can git graphs like the above in your terminal if you add `--graph` to the `git log` command; i.e.

   ```bash
   git log --graph
   git log title-dev --graph
   ```
   :::

1. Add the following lines to `story.txt`:

   ```bash

   It is period of civil war.
   Rebel spaceships, striking
   from a hidden base, have won
   their first victory against
   the evil Galactic Empire.
   ```

   Stage the change and commit it:

   ```bash
   git add -u
   git commit -m "add intro paragraph"
   ```

   Now type `git log`: you should have 3 commits, none of which include the commits to `title-dev` branch.

1. Move back to the `title-dev` branch:

   ```bash
   git checkout title-dev
   ```

   Modify the content of `title.txt` to be:

   ```bash
   Star Wars
   A NEW HOPE

   by
   George Lucas
   ```

   Stage the change and commit it:

   ```bash
   git add -u
   git commit -m "update title"
   ```

   `git log` shows 4 commits: the first two from `main` (before you branched off), and the last two on `title-dev`.

1. Go back to the `main` branch:

   ```bash
   git checkout main
   ```

   Merge the changes from `title-dev`:

   ```bash
   git merge title-dev
   ```

   This will open up your text editor. Don't change the commit message, just save and exit to finish the merge and return to the terminal.

   `git log` should show 6 commits: the initial two commits on main, the first commit on title-dev, the `add paragraph` commit on `main`, the `update title` commit on `title-dev`, followed by an additional "merge" commit. This final "merge" commit is to indicate that some of the commits in the history came from another branch (and what the name of the branch was).

   `ls` now shows that both `story.txt` and `title.txt` are in your directory and both have the most up-to-date versions.

1. Delete the `title-dev` branch to save space now that it is merged:

   ```bash
   git branch -d title-dev
   ```

### Part 4: Resolving merge conflicts

1. Set up `list.txt`, `dev1`, and `dev2` as described in the [Challenge Questions](../exercise1.qmd#challenge-questions-editing-the-same-file-on-different-branches).

   ::: {.callout-tip title="Challenge Questions via the command line" collapse="true"}
   ```bash
   # Question 1
   printf 'alpha\nbravo\ncharlie\n' > list.txt
   git add list.txt
   git commit -m "add list"
   git checkout -b dev1
   printf 'delta\nbravo\ncharlie\n' > list.txt
   git commit -am "add delta to list"
   git checkout main
   printf 'alpha\nbravo\nfoxtrot\n' > list.txt
   git commit -am "add foxtrot to list"

   # Question 2
   git merge dev1

   # Question 3
   git checkout -b dev2
   printf 'delta\necho\nfoxtrot\n' > list.txt
   git commit -am "add echo to list"
   git checkout main
   printf 'delta\neasy\nfoxtrot\n' > list.txt
   git commit -am "add easy to list"
   ```
   :::

   Then merge `dev2` into `main`:

   ```bash
   git checkout main
   git merge dev2
   ```

   You should get:

   ```txt
   Auto-merging list.txt
   CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in list.txt
   Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
   ```

   `git status` lists `list.txt` under `Unmerged paths` as `both modified`.

1. Open `list.txt` in your text editor. You should see:

   ```txt
   delta
   <<<<<<< HEAD
   easy
   =======
   echo
   >>>>>>> dev2
   foxtrot
   ```

   The lines between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` are the version on `main` (the branch being merged into), the lines between `=======` and `>>>>>>> dev2` are the version on `dev2`.

1. Keep the version from `dev2`: delete the markers and the `easy` line so that the file looks like:

   ```txt
   delta
   echo
   foxtrot
   ```

   Then save and exit the file.

1. Stage the file and complete the merge *without* the `-m`:

   ```bash
   git add list.txt
   git commit
   ```

   This opens your text editor with the commit message set to `Merge branch 'dev2'`. Save and exit. `git log` now shows the merge commit, as if you had merged without any issue.
